listening.title: University Language-Partner Matching Scheme
listening.focus: Understanding paraphrase, linked ideas and corrected details in an academic discussion
listening.script:
Maya: Hi Jon, have you signed up for the university's language-partner matching scheme this term?
Jon: Yes, I applied last week. I wanted to improve my Spanish, so they matched me with Sofia, an exchange student from Argentina.
Maya: That's great. I requested a Mandarin partner because I'm going to Beijing on an exchange programme next year and I need more speaking practice.
Jon: How often do you meet? Sofia and I meet twice a week, for about an hour each time in the main library.
Maya: Same here. We use the conversation room on the second floor. We divide the hour equally — thirty minutes in English and thirty minutes in Mandarin.
Jon: We do the same, thirty minutes per language. The coordinator, Dr Evans, told us to prepare a topic before each meeting, like hobbies, food, or travel plans.
Maya: Right, and we have to keep a short weekly log of what we talked about and any new vocabulary. It's not marked, but she reviews it to give advice.
Jon: I thought the log had to be sent every Friday, but actually the email says it's due every Sunday evening.
Maya: Thanks for correcting me — I had Friday in my notes too. Do you also go to the monthly group session?
Jon: Yes, the first one is next Thursday at four o'clock in Room B. I initially thought it was Wednesday, but the updated timetable shows Thursday.
Maya: I'll be there. I heard the coordinator discusses common difficulties, such as speaking too quickly or not asking follow-up questions.
Jon: And she offers extra pronunciation workshops for anyone who wants them. I'm considering joining the Spanish one.
Maya: Me too for Mandarin. Overall, I think this scheme is much more helpful than just using a language app, because you have real interaction.
Jon: I agree. I've only had three meetings, but I already feel more confident speaking.

reading.title: Riverside Neighbourhood Library Delivery Trial
reading.focus: Following linked ideas, comparisons, and distinguishing claims from examples
reading.passage:
Riverside Neighbourhood Library began a three-month home delivery trial in January to help residents who find it difficult to visit the building. The library wanted to reach older people, parents with young children, and shift workers with limited free time. Before the trial, these groups borrowed fewer books than regular visitors, even though surveys showed they wanted to read more.

The service was simple. Residents could request up to five items at a time through the library website or by telephone. A small team of trained volunteers then delivered books to homes twice a week, on Tuesdays and Fridays. Each delivery included a return bag for books that were finished. The loan period was the same as in the library — three weeks — and users received a reminder message two days before the due date. Unlike the normal self-service system, volunteers also offered brief recommendations based on previous choices.

By the end of March, 120 households had used the delivery service at least once. A questionnaire showed that 85% of users were satisfied or very satisfied, and many said they read more often than before. However, the trial also revealed problems. About one in five deliveries was returned late, often because users forgot the collection day. In addition, the volunteer team was sometimes too small to cover all requests quickly, especially during the school holidays in February when two volunteers were away.

The library compared delivery users with people who continued to visit in person. Both groups borrowed a similar number of books on average, but delivery users tried a wider range of genres. For example, regular visitors mostly chose fiction, while delivery users more often added history, science, and cookery books after receiving suggestions. This suggests that personal recommendations had a positive effect, although the library notes that delivery users may already have had broader interests.

One example often mentioned is Mrs Lee, a 72-year-old resident who had not visited the library for two years due to mobility issues. Through the trial, she received large-print novels and audiobooks every two weeks and said the service reduced her sense of isolation. Her experience illustrates an individual benefit, but the library's overall claim is that the trial was successful because it increased access without reducing the quality of the service. To continue, the library states it will need stable funding to pay for transport and to recruit more volunteers. The council will decide in June whether to extend the scheme for another year.

exercises.title: Riverside Neighbourhood Library Delivery Trial
exercises.focus: Following linked ideas, comparisons, and distinguishing claims from examples
exercises.passage:
Riverside Neighbourhood Library began a three-month home delivery trial in January to help residents who find it difficult to visit the building. The library wanted to reach older people, parents with young children, and shift workers with limited free time. Before the trial, these groups borrowed fewer books than regular visitors, even though surveys showed they wanted to read more.

The service was simple. Residents could request up to five items at a time through the library website or by telephone. A small team of trained volunteers then delivered books to homes twice a week, on Tuesdays and Fridays. Each delivery included a return bag for books that were finished. The loan period was the same as in the library — three weeks — and users received a reminder message two days before the due date. Unlike the normal self-service system, volunteers also offered brief recommendations based on previous choices.

By the end of March, 120 households had used the delivery service at least once. A questionnaire showed that 85% of users were satisfied or very satisfied, and many said they read more often than before. However, the trial also revealed problems. About one in five deliveries was returned late, often because users forgot the collection day. In addition, the volunteer team was sometimes too small to cover all requests quickly, especially during the school holidays in February when two volunteers were away.

The library compared delivery users with people who continued to visit in person. Both groups borrowed a similar number of books on average, but delivery users tried a wider range of genres. For example, regular visitors mostly chose fiction, while delivery users more often added history, science, and cookery books after receiving suggestions. This suggests that personal recommendations had a positive effect, although the library notes that delivery users may already have had broader interests.

One example often mentioned is Mrs Lee, a 72-year-old resident who had not visited the library for two years due to mobility issues. Through the trial, she received large-print novels and audiobooks every two weeks and said the service reduced her sense of isolation. Her experience illustrates an individual benefit, but the library's overall claim is that the trial was successful because it increased access without reducing the quality of the service. To continue, the library states it will need stable funding to pay for transport and to recruit more volunteers. The council will decide in June whether to extend the scheme for another year.
exercises.prompt: What was the main purpose of the delivery trial?
options: To increase access for residents unable to visit
To reduce number of visitors to library
To test a new library website
exercises.explanation: The passage states the trial aimed to help those who find visiting difficult. Reducing visitors contradicts the stated aim of increasing access.

writingPrompts.focus: Paraphrase and compare participation data across familiar workshop topics
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the number of participants in three session types at the Riverside Community Workshop in 2022 and 2023, and the percentage of participants who said they would return.

Riverside Community Workshop:
2022 - Woodwork: 120 participants, 68% would return | Digital Skills: 95 participants, 72% would return | Gardening: 80 participants, 85% would return
2023 - Woodwork: 135 participants, 75% would return | Digital Skills: 140 participants, 78% would return | Gardening: 110 participants, 82% would return

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Public Transport Information Campaign Survey
writingPrompts.focus: Correct details and clear comparisons from survey results before and after a campaign
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the results of a survey of 500 residents in Westfield City before and after a public transport information campaign in March 2023. The survey asked if people were aware of three services.

Percentage who answered Yes, I am aware:
Before campaign (February 2023) - City Bus Map: 42% | Mobile Ticket App: 35% | Night Bus Service: 28%
After campaign (April 2023) - City Bus Map: 61% | Mobile Ticket App: 58% | Night Bus Service: 44%

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

writingPrompts.focus: Linked ideas and balanced comparison of two views on alumni advice
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people think college alumni panels are very useful for current students when choosing a career. Others think advice from former students is often outdated and not relevant to today's job market.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Funding for Shared Community Workshops
writingPrompts.focus: Paraphrase the issue and develop a clear position with linked reasons
writingPrompts.prompt:
Many local councils fund shared community workshops where people can learn practical skills such as woodwork, repair, and digital skills together. Some people argue this money should be spent on traditional classroom education instead.

To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Effectiveness of Public Transport Campaigns
writingPrompts.focus: Evaluation and comparison of effectiveness with corrected detail and examples
writingPrompts.prompt:
Public transport information campaigns often encourage people to use buses and trains instead of cars. Some people believe these campaigns are effective in changing travel habits, while others think they have little impact.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 1 · Daily Travel and Public Transport
speakingPrompts.focus: Paraphrase and give short linked answers on familiar travel topics
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about travel and public transport.
- How do you usually travel to college or work?
- How often do you use buses or trains?
- Is public transport information clear in your city?
- Would you like to use public transport more in the future?

speakingPrompts.focus: Corrected details and simple comparisons about learning experiences
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about learning new skills.
- What kind of practical skills would you like to learn?
- Do you prefer learning alone or with other people?
- Have you ever attended a workshop or training session?
- How useful is it to learn from people with experience?

speakingPrompts.focus: Describe a workshop or talk with clear structure and linked ideas
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a talk or workshop you attended at your college or in your community, such as an alumni panel or a community workshop.
You should say:
- what the event was and when it happened
- who organised it and who spoke
- what you learned or did there
- and explain how useful it was for you

You will have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Value of Alumni Panels and Community Learning
speakingPrompts.focus: Reasons and evaluation of different ways of learning from others
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's consider community learning more broadly.
- Why do some students find advice from alumni more helpful than advice from teachers?
- What are the advantages and disadvantages of learning practical skills in a shared workshop compared to learning online?
- How can colleges make alumni panels more useful for all students?
- Do you think community workshops can help people of different ages learn from each other? Why or why not?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Public Information Campaigns and Behaviour Change
speakingPrompts.focus: Evaluation and comparison of campaign methods and their impact
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Let's talk about public information campaigns.
- Why do some public transport campaigns succeed in changing behaviour while others do not?
